title: Hilbert: Recursively Building Formal Proofs with Informal Reasoning
one_liner: An agent that splits hard math proofs into simpler pieces, asks LLMs to solve each piece either informally or formally, and glues them back together with verification.
lead: Large language models are great at explaining math in everyday words, but they make mistakes that we cannot prove wrong. Formal proof systems like Lean 4 verify proofs with total precision, but current models trained for formal reasoning solve fewer problems than those using plain English. Hilbert closes this gap by building an agent that combines both: it thinks informally to break problems apart, then asks specialized models to formally verify each piece.

problem.h2: Why math proofs are hard for LLMs
paras: Large language models can explain mathematics in plain English—they can reason through steps and suggest ideas. But here is the catch: they make subtle mistakes. A mathematician checking the proof on paper might catch them, but a model has no way to know if it went wrong.

The fix seems obvious: make a specialized model that outputs proofs in Lean 4, a formal system where the computer itself checks every step automatically. If the proof compiles, it is correct. But there is a tradeoff: models trained to output formal Lean code solve only half as many problems as models working in plain English. You get certainty but lose the reasoning muscle.

A beginner might try training a single model to do both at once, but formal and informal reasoning require opposite skills—one needs to be concise and exact, the other exploratory and flexible. That model would fail at both.

callout.html: Informal reasoning can find the solution but makes mistakes; formal proofs are airtight but hard to generate. Current models cannot do both.

panels.title: 1. The two worlds
panels.caption: Informal models reason flexibly but may err. Formal models verify perfectly but solve fewer problems.

panels.title: 2. A hard proof problem arrives
panels.caption: A proof task lands. One model alone is not enough.

panels.title: 3. Hilbert decomposes the problem
panels.caption: Agent splits the theorem into smaller subgoals recursively using informal reasoning.

panels.title: 4. Each piece is proven formally
panels.caption: Formal verifier checks each subgoal. If one fails, informal reasoner refines it.

panels.title: 5. Proofs glued back together
panels.caption: Subproofs chain together into a complete formal proof that Lean 4 certifies.

steps.text: When the formal prover gets stuck, Hilbert asks an informal LLM: break this into smaller pieces.

steps.b: Attempt formal proof of each piece
steps.text: For each subgoal, a specialized Lean-trained model generates formal proof tactics (Lean code).
Lean 4 runs the proof. Either it compiles (success) or fails with an error message.
If a subproof fails, the error message goes back to the informal reasoner to reframe that piece.
Repeat decompose-and-verify until the whole theorem is formally proven or declared unsolvable.

paras: Hilbert changes where the reasoning happens. Instead of asking one model to do both informal and formal reasoning, it splits the labor: the informal model handles decomposition and refinement (the exploratory thinking), and the formal model focuses only on translating individual subgoals into Lean tactics (the mechanical translation). The verifier provides feedback that flows back to the informal reasoner, creating a loop.

hidden.h2: The proof tree depth and branching
hidden.name: decomposition fanout and recursion depth
paras: The hidden quantity here is how much the problem has been broken down. A theorem that requires only one or two decompositions is easier than one that needs five levels of nesting or dozens of subgoals at each level. This is not mentioned in the abstract, but it matters deeply: if decomposition creates too many pieces, the formal prover drowns in them; if it decomposes too little, the pieces stay too hard for formal tactics.

Hilbert measures this implicitly through the verifier feedback: if a subgoal fails, the agent knows decomposition did not go deep enough, and the informal reasoner is asked to try again. The depth of the recursion tree is thus the hidden signal that guides whether the strategy is working.

heat.caption: Darker means deeper recursion; highlighted shows proved subgoals. Depth must be tuned to avoid bottleneck.

reads.html: Think of a huge puzzle. If you try to solve it as one piece, it is impossible. But if you break it into 10 chunks and solve each chunk, the chunks are solvable. Hilbert decides how deep to break. Too shallow, chunks are still hard. Too deep, you have a thousand tiny pieces. The right depth makes each piece formal-solvable without creating a combinatorial explosion.

The paper does not use the term, but the effective branching factor and recursion depth of the decomposition tree directly determine whether subgoals are within the formal prover's capability. This is governed by the informal reasoner's strategy, which adapts based on verifier failure signals.

mechanism.h2: Why informal-then-formal works better than formal-only
paras: The reason Hilbert outperforms a formal-only prover is that it recruits the informal model's reasoning strength before invoking formal verification. Informal reasoning excels because it can make long chains of logical leaps and explore multiple pathways; it is fast and flexible. Formal reasoning is bulletproof because Lean checks every single step, but it is slow and has a narrow range of tactics it knows how to apply.

By using the informal model to decompose the problem first, Hilbert narrows the scope of what the formal prover must do. Each subgoal is easier than the original problem, so the formal prover is more likely to find a valid tactic sequence. When a subgoal does fail, the informal reasoner does not just give up—it learns from the Lean error message and tries a different decomposition. This feedback loop exploits the informal model's adaptability.

The verifier's role is critical: it surfaces exactly which pieces are stuck, so the informal reasoner knows where to refine. Without this signal, decomposition would be random. With it, decomposition becomes targeted and improves with each failed attempt, because the informal reasoner sees the exact Lean error message and can adjust—breaking that subgoal differently, or changing how it frames the logical requirements.

stages.s: Hard theorem that formal prover alone cannot solve
Formal prover generates Lean tactics for each subgoal
Failed subgoals sent back to informal reasoner
Complete formal proof verified by Lean 4

math.words: Let S be the original theorem statement. If the formal prover cannot directly prove S, decompose it into subgoals G_1, G_2, ..., G_n. For each G_i, attempt formal proof. If G_i fails with error message E_i, ask the informal reasoner to refine or re-decompose G_i into G_i1, G_i2, ... and recurse. The depth d_i of the recursion tree for G_i is a proxy for decomposition adequacy. A subgoal is solvable if d_i remains bounded and the formal prover finds a tactic sequence.
math.equation: solved(S) = all G_i at depth d_i are formally verified, where d_i >= 1, max(d_i) < D_max
symbols: the original theorem statement to prove
the i-th subgoal after one decomposition
how many levels of recursive decomposition subgoal i required
the maximum depth before giving up (prevents infinite loops)
the error message from Lean when subgoal i fails
true if all subgoals are formally proved; false if any subgoal is unsolvable

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Theorem: Prove property P on set X (too hard for formal prover directly).
Decomposition 1: Break into subgoals P_A (prove on subset A) and P_B (prove on subset B).
Formal attempt on P_A: fails with error 'tactic did not close goal'. Recursion depth d_A = 1.
Informal re-reasoning on P_A: decomposes further into P_A1 and P_A2.
Formal attempt on P_A1: succeeds. Formal attempt on P_A2: succeeds. Recursion depth d_A = 2.
Similarly, P_B decomposes and verifies at depth d_B = 1.
All subgoals proved: max(d_A, d_B) = 2 < D_max. Original theorem P solved.

math.note: The depth represents how many times the informal reasoner had to refine a subgoal; bounded depth means the strategy is working efficiently.

charts.title: Formal-only prover baseline
charts.note: A specialized formal prover alone solves about half of the benchmark problems. Verification is airtight, but it cannot reason flexibly enough.

charts.title: Hilbert (informal + formal + verifier)
charts.note: Hilbert's decomposition + feedback loop solves nearly twice as many theorems. The informal reasoner's flexibility guides the formal prover to success.

items.html: If the informal reasoner breaks a problem into too many pieces or nests too deeply, the sheer number of subgoals overwhelms the system. It runs out of time or memory before the formal prover can verify them all.
A subgoal is truly unsolvable, but the informal reasoner keeps trying new decompositions. Without a hard bound on recursion depth D_max, the system hangs.

items.b: Formal prover stuck on a solvable subgoal.
items.html: A subgoal is decomposed perfectly, but the formal prover does not have the right Lean tactic in its training. Verifier reports failure, and the informal reasoner re-decomposes, but the core issue is that the formal model is weak.

The informal reasoner makes smart decompositions that match the theorem's logical structure. Each subgoal is just barely within the formal prover's capability. The verifier catches mistakes early. The recursion depth stays under D_max. The full proof is solved in reasonable time and verified by Lean 4.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A demo should show a concrete theorem (e.g. a combinatorial identity or a number-theory property) that the formal prover alone cannot prove. Then run Hilbert and show the decomposition tree: which subgoals were created, how deep the recursion went, and which subgoals required re-reasoning. Finally, display the final Lean 4 proof that Lean verifies as correct.
demo.metric_eq: success_rate = (theorems_solved_by_Hilbert) / (theorems_solved_by_formal_only) = fraction by which Hilbert improves on the baseline
demo.closing: The demo must make it impossible to miss that decomposition plus feedback enables the formal prover to tackle problems it could never handle alone (because each subgoal is smaller and within the prover's capability), and that Lean 4 certifies every result.
